Aloud
uh-LOWD
adv.
From a- plus loud. Webster 1828: loudly; with a strong voice or great noise. In the Authorized Version it belongs chiefly to two activities — praise and prophetic warning — and in both the volume is commanded rather than merely permitted.

Biblical Definition

Aloud in Scripture is not enthusiasm but obedience; God repeatedly commands audible worship and audible warning. The psalms are full of it: Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob (Psalm 81:1); I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning (Psalm 59:16); my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness (Psalm 51:14, David’s vow after his sin); let the saints be joyful in glory: let them sing aloud upon their beds (Psalm 149:5). It is also the volume of prayer under pressure: Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice (Psalm 55:17). And it is the prophet’s commission: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins (Isaiah 58:1) — where the volume and the content are commanded together, and the content is sin named to the people who are committing it. Job’s complaint is the other side of it: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment (Job 19:7). The word assumes a God who hears and a congregation that can be heard.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ALOUD as loudly; with a loud voice or great noise. The KJV uses it of singing, of crying to God in prayer, and of the prophet’s public rebuke.

expand to see more

ALOUD, adv. — Loudly; with a loud voice, or great noise.

The word implies audibility to others, not merely volume; to cry aloud is to be heard by those present.

That is why Isaiah 58:1 pairs it with a trumpet. The prophet’s rebuke is not a private conviction but a public declaration that the people cannot claim they did not hear.

Key Scripture

Psalm 51:14 — "Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness."

Psalm 55:17 — "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice."

Psalm 81:1 — "To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of Asaph. Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob."

Isaiah 58:1 — "Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins."

Job 19:7 — "Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment."

Modern Corruption

The corruption is on both sides of the volume: congregational praise reduced to a performance the people watch in silence, and prophetic rebuke muted into inoffensiveness so that Isaiah 58:1 is obeyed in neither its loudness nor its content.

expand to see more

Psalm 81:1 and Psalm 149:5 assume a people who sing. Congregational psalmody was one of the Reformation’s recoveries precisely because the medieval church had moved the singing from the pews to the choir, and it is worth noticing how easily that reverses. Where the volume comes from the platform and the congregation listens, the command to sing aloud unto God our strength is being performed on the people’s behalf rather than obeyed by them. The regulative principle bears on this: God has commanded His people to sing, and a service arranged so that they need not is not more reverent but less obedient.

Isaiah 58:1 is the harder half. The command is to cry aloud, to spare not, to sound like a trumpet, and to shew my people their transgression — and the people in view are God’s own, in the middle of a fast they think is going well. Preaching that has decided in advance never to name a sin its hearers actually commit has kept the volume and lost the commission, or more often lost both. The prophet is not licensed to be cruel; the chapter goes on to promise light rising in obscurity and a rebuilt city. But the promise comes after the naming, and no amount of warmth later excuses silence now.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The English adverb renders Hebrew expressions of loud voice — commonly ranan, to give a ringing cry, and the phrase begaron, with the throat, in Isaiah 58:1.

expand to see more

Hebrew ranan (H7442) — to give a ringing cry, to shout for joy; behind sing aloud in Psalm 51:14, 59:16, and 81:1.

Hebrew qara' begaron — literally call with the throat; Isaiah 58:1, rendered cry aloud.

Hebrew shophar (H7782) — the trumpet Isaiah names as the standard of the prophet’s volume.

Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, roar, be in tumult; behind the crying aloud of Psalm 55:17.

The KJV distinguishes crying aloud from crying out; the first is deliberate publication, the second often distress.

Usage

"Sing aloud unto God our strength (Psalm 81:1) — congregational praise commanded, not merely allowed."

"Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud (Psalm 55:17) — fixed hours and an audible voice."

"Cry aloud, spare not… shew my people their transgression (Isaiah 58:1) — the volume and the content commanded in one breath."
